title: Files and Directories
story:
Your first week on the JumpToTech Bank platform team, and you have been given a shell on a build host. Before anyone hands you a production system, your team lead wants to see that you can move around a filesystem and put files where they belong without asking which button to press.
The task is small on purpose. Everything that follows in this track — reading logs, fixing permissions, writing scripts — assumes you can do this without thinking about it.
objectives: Find out where you are in the filesystem and list what is there
Create directories and empty files from the command line
Move a file into another directory and confirm it is no longer in the old one

task.summary: Build a small project directory tree and move a log file into an archive.
task.description:
Your shell starts in the `student` account's home directory. Everything in this task happens inside it, and you already own it, so nothing here needs elevated privileges.
Create a directory called `project` in your home directory. Inside it, create two empty files, `app.log` and `config.txt`. Then create an `archive` directory inside `project`, and move `app.log` into it.
When you are done, `project` should contain `config.txt` and the `archive` directory, and `archive` should contain `app.log`. Note the word "move": a copy that leaves the original behind is not the same thing, and this lab checks for that.

requirements: config.txt is in the project directory
The archive directory exists inside project
app.log is in the archive directory

hints.text: Two of these steps make something that did not exist before, and one moves something that did. Think about which command family each belongs to, and remember that a directory and a file are created by different commands.

The GNU Coreutils manual documents the commands for creating directories and empty files, and for renaming or relocating them. `man mkdir`, `man touch`, and `man mv` are also available right there in your terminal. If you are unsure where you are, there is a command that prints the working directory.

The final layout must be exactly `~/project/config.txt`, `~/project/archive/`, and `~/project/archive/app.log`. Check your work with `ls -R ~/project`. If `app.log` still appears directly under `project` as well as under `archive`, you copied it instead of moving it — the last check exists precisely to catch that.

references.title: GNU Coreutils — Directory listing and file creation
